rows.sourceExcerpt: Social communication can reduce duplication while increasing shared bias. A widely repeated theory may steer volunteers away from places that contradict it. responseBinding.questionText: Why should a checked sector include a confidence indication?
responseBinding.correctOptionText: Because inspections differ in thoroughness and visibility

rows.sourceExcerpt: A sector board can show which areas have been assigned, checked or left open. It need not dictate exactly how each person searches. Its purpose is to expose coverage gaps and allow new volunteers to choose neglected areas. Updates must be easy to submit, otherwise the board becomes a delayed picture of yesterday’s effort. Equally, a checked label should not imply certainty when the inspection was brief or visibility was poor. Status needs both location and confidence.

responseBinding.questionText: What determines how much verification a report needs?
responseBinding.correctOptionText: The cost of acting on a mistaken report

rows.sourceExcerpt: Crowds generate candidate sightings as well as search coverage. These reports vary greatly in quality. Sending every one directly to field teams can overwhelm the operation, so evidence may enter a verification queue. Clear photographs, precise locations or agreement between independent observers can raise priority. Verification protects scarce response capacity, but excessive delay can make good information useless. The process must match scrutiny to the cost of acting on an error.

responseBinding.questionText: What problem can occur if every report is sent to a specialist?

rows.sourceExcerpt: Volunteers offer scale and familiarity with local conditions; specialists may recognise technical evidence or manage risk. Mixed teams can combine these strengths. Yet expertise should be deployed where it changes decisions rather than used as a ceremonial label. A specialist reviewing thousands of low-information reports becomes a bottleneck. Triage, training and structured forms can help contributors supply the details that an expert needs to make a rapid judgement.

responseBinding.questionText: Which phrase best captures the author’s preferred design?

rows.sourceExcerpt: The value of a crowd lies neither in raw numbers nor in central control alone. Effective search combines coordinated diversity: enough structure to reveal gaps and verify reports, enough independence to test different possibilities. Platforms shape this balance through assignment, updates, confidence labels and feedback. They cannot guarantee recovery, because the evidence may never be present or observable. They can, however, turn scattered goodwill into a search whose limits and coverage are understood.

responseBinding.questionText: The author believes that the number of volunteers alone determines search quality.

rows.sourceExcerpt: When an object is lost across a large physical or digital space, a single searcher may inspect only a small fraction. Crowdsourcing can divide the task among many contributors. At first glance, more eyes should mean greater coverage. That expectation is reasonable only if effort is distributed. A thousand volunteers who all examine the most obvious location may add less value than a small team assigned to distinct sectors. The problem is therefore one of coordination as well as participation.

rows.sourceExcerpt: Uncoordinated searchers sometimes bring a useful advantage: independent strategies. Different people notice different cues and question different assumptions. If every volunteer follows the same detailed hunch, the search becomes vulnerable to a shared mistake. Diversity can broaden coverage, but complete independence also creates duplication. The challenge is to preserve varied judgement while making completed work visible enough to prevent needless repetition.
